meta.title: Amharic B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 494 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Amharic → English (see the Amharic, recall the meaning) and English → Amharic (see an English meaning, recall the Amharic). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 494 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. THIS LEVEL IS SHORT: a B1 deck would hold about 1,000 words, and this one holds 494, because that is what English Wiktionary has left after A1 and A2 — the rest of its Amharic words, many of them concrete and rarer (tools, animals, plants, spices). There is no B2 for the same reason. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Amharic, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 24 of the 494 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — health and the body, the home and the table, money and doing things, the world about us, and describing people and things — and the other 470 are the commonest remaining words of the Amharic Wikipedia, counted by the WHOLE word: Amharic writes its prepositions and endings onto the word (ቤት 'house', ቤቱ 'the house', በቤቱ 'in the house'), so those forms are added together. That corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (history, government, religion), and verbs are counted less well than nouns, so they rank lower than they are used. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and some of the commonest are missing from it (አዎ 'yes', እና 'and', ግን 'but', ለምን 'why', ሄደ 'to go'). Every word is in the Ethiopic script (fidäl), as Amharic is written; the Fidäl deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters. Beneath it is Wiktionary's romanisation, which also marks the doubled consonants the script leaves unwritten. A verb is shown by its dictionary form, the past 'he did' (ገዛ 'he bought', taught as 'to buy'), with its infinitive where Wiktionary gives one; a few verbs Wiktionary has only as an infinitive are taught by that (መምጣት 'to come'). A noun shows its gender, plural and definite form where Wiktionary has them. Several Amharic letters are said alike (ሀ ሐ ኀ, ሰ ሠ, አ ዐ, ጸ ፀ), so many words have two or three spellings; the card heads with the one the Amharic Wikipedia uses most and names the others. Example sentences are few: 6 of the 494 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 250 Amharic sentences with a translation; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have an Amharic voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Amharic Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
